public_rationale: Errors are documented, and survey evidence connects hallucination concerns with less favorable attitudes and continued-use intentions. Neither establishes Marcus's complete causal claim: that unreliability limits payments from many OpenAI customers and thereby contributes to its profitability difficulties. Improvements in reliability also caution against treating all products and tasks alike. The available evidence does not establish the opposite causal conclusion either.
limitations: General AI survey findings do not directly measure OpenAI purchasing behavior.

statement.excerpt: One thing that Noble doesn’t mention is why OpenAI has struggled to make a profit; in my eyes, there are three reasons, that I have emphasized here before: the product is unreliable (placing an upper bound on how much many people be willing to pay), it is expensive to operate, and they have no technical moat, which has led to price wars.

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that product errors materially reduce willingness to pay among a substantial group of potential customers, contributing to OpenAI's profitability difficulties.
Marcus does not claim that unreliability is the only cause, or that nobody will pay.
Use calendar 2025, the latest completed annual financial period before publication, for the profitability component. Product evidence must concern products available before the post.
No accounting measure or basis is specified. Do not substitute cash burn or gross margin for net profit.
'In my eyes' identifies an opinion about an empirical causal relationship; it is not a forecast condition.

criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative customer evidence and a financial analysis establish that reliability shortcomings did not materially constrain willingness to pay or contribute to the profitability difficulties described.
